qs.q: A patient presents with subacute pericarditis. Based on the classification, how long have the symptoms been present?
qs.e: Subacute pericarditis is classified as lasting from 6 weeks to 6 months, whereas acute pericarditis is less than 6 weeks and chronic is greater than 6 months. It can present with effusive-constrictive features.

qs.q: Which of the following is categorized under the metabolic causes of pericarditis?
qs.e: Uremia and hypothyroidism are metabolic causes of pericarditis, whereas Coxsackievirus is infectious and Rheumatoid arthritis is autoimmune. Neoplasms like Hodgkin's disease form a separate etiologic category.

qs.q: During auscultation of a patient with suspected acute pericarditis, a high-pitched scratchy or squeaky sound is best heard with the diaphragm at the left sternal border. What does this friction rub correspond to?
o: Atrial systole, ventricular systole, and early diastole
Isovolumetric contraction, rapid ejection, and atrial kick
First heart sound, second heart sound, and a third heart sound
Ventricular filling, passive diastole, and atrial repolarization
qs.e: A pericardial friction rub has three components which correspond to atrial systole, ventricular systole, and early diastole. It is a key sign present in a majority of acute pericarditis cases.

qs.q: An ECG is performed on a patient in the first few hours of acute pericarditis. Which of the following findings is characteristic of Stage 1?
o: Diffuse ST elevation with a concave configuration
Normalization of ST and PR segments
Complete resolution of all electrical activity
qs.e: Stage 1 of acute pericarditis is characterized by diffuse ST elevation with a concave configuration occurring within the first hours to days. Subsequent stages involve normalization, T wave inversions, and eventual recovery.

qs.q: A patient with acute pericarditis is prescribed NSAIDs. Why are corticosteroids generally considered second-line therapy for inflammation in this condition?
o: Corticosteroids are associated with a high incidence of recurrence.
Corticosteroids fail to reduce systemic inflammation entirely.
Corticosteroids always cause immediate renal failure.
Corticosteroids are too expensive for routine outpatient use.
qs.e: Steroids have shown an incidence of high recurrence of pericarditis, thus they should be given as second-line therapy or when NSAIDs are contraindicated. They are also strictly contraindicated in uremic pericarditis.

qs.q: Which of the following medications is used as an add-on therapy to NSAIDs specifically to reduce the incidence of recurrence in pericarditis?
qs.e: Colchicine is used as an add-on to NSAIDs to reduce the incidence of recurrence, though it shares contraindications in peptic ulcer disease and end-stage renal disease. Prednisone is a corticosteroid, while aspirin and indomethacin are standard NSAIDs.

qs.q: Which of the following clinical findings or patient histories mandates hospitalization for a patient with acute pericarditis?
o: Fever greater than 38 degrees Celsius and leukocytosis
Immediate improvement within 24 hours of starting ibuprofen
Absence of any previous anticoagulant therapy
qs.e: Criteria for hospitalization include fever greater than 38 degrees Celsius and leukocytosis, evidence of cardiac tamponade, a large effusion >20mm, immunosuppression, oral anticoagulant therapy, trauma, failure to respond to NSAIDs, and elevated troponin.

qs.q: A 66-year-old man has a friction rub on chest auscultation, BUN of 100 mg/dL, and creatinine of 9.8 mg/dL. Most likely form of pericarditis?
qs.e: Severe uremia from renal failure triggers fibrin exudation onto pericardial surfaces, producing fibrinous pericarditis with a classic friction rub on auscultation.

ai.summary: Pericarditis is inflammation of the pericardial sac that causes chest pain, friction rub, and ECG changes. It can be acute, subacute, or chronic, and may progress to tamponade or constriction.

sections.p: Pericarditis is diagnosed by a combination of clinical features, ECG, echocardiography, and inflammatory markers. Classic ECG shows diffuse ST elevation and PR depression.

sections.p: Severity is staged by clinical presentation and imaging. Stage 1: acute, uncomplicated. Stage 2: effusive or tamponade. Stage 3: constrictive.

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, infections dominate. Viral (e.g., enterovirus) is most common, followed by bacterial (TB, HIV), rheumatic fever, and post‑MI.

sections.p: Urgent complications include cardiac tamponade, constrictive pericarditis, and sudden death. Red flags are dyspnea, hypotension, pulsus paradoxus, and muffled heart sounds.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first. NSAIDs or colchicine reduce inflammation; steroids are reserved for refractory or autoimmune cases. Drainage is required for tamponade.
